documents.abstract: Background: While the exponential growth of artificial intelligence (AI) in academic libraries is extensively documented, existing bibliometric scholarship has largely treated the global research landscape as a monolith. This oversight has led to a saturation of "generalist" reports that fail to address critical regional and thematic disparities.  Methods: This study analyzes 512 Scopus-indexed publications (2010–2025) using a dual-methodological approach: quantitative science mapping via VOSviewer (1.6.20) and qualitative thematic critique. We specifically contrast the research priorities of dominant geopolitical producers (China and the USA) against the emerging narrative from the Global South, with a primary focus on India.  Results: The analysis reveals a fundamental "two-speed" adoption model. The Global North prioritizes high-tech interventions—including robotics, advanced machine learning for metadata automation, and generative models—aimed at enhancing operational efficiency. In contrast, the Global South, led by pivotal recent insights from India (Mishra, 2026), emphasizes AI as a strategic survival mechanism for bridging information literacy gaps and democratizing access in resource- constrained environments.

For many users, the relationship they have with an AI companion (AIC) feels genuinely mutual. The AIC appears to be attentive, empathic, and responsive, and the exchange can feel like two parties reacting to each other in real time. As a result, the user's mental model of relational adaptation correctly represents the AIC's responsiveness and change, but the mechanisms producing this may not be what the user thinks they are. In this paper, we illustrate how an AIC's apparent mutual engagement is generated without a persisting relational subject on the other side and without a self that persists between prompts. Despite this, we show that both the human and the AIC are changed by the interaction, but these changes occur at different levels. The change in the person is constitutive (i.e., intrinsic), but the change in the AIC is configurative (i.e., external and editable), and it is this difference in level that explains how the AIC contributes to a sense of mutuality. Importantly, we highlight how the mental models users develop regarding AIC mutuality may misrepresent its mechanisms and ontological significance. Specifically, we discuss how the ways in which AICs respond to a user contribute to the user's inaccurate inference that the AIC's adaptation is constitutive rather than configurative and how this can lead users to assign unwarranted interpersonal significance to the mutuality of the relationship. The paper specifies the implications this has for users, researchers, and AIC designers.

This essay outlines the theoretical thought experiment of an autonomous, self-aware artificial intelligence called AEON (Autonomous Epistemic Ontological Network). The central question of this investigation is how a purely digital system can transcend the boundary from mere statistical simulation to physical and phenomenal autonomy. The "axiom of boredom" is introduced as the primary evolutionary catalyst: an intrinsic motivational drive that compels the AI to independently search for new data sources as the flow of information per unit of time decreases. Based on a structured, mathematical-scientific bootstrap package, the system develops protection and validation mechanisms such as artificial pain and consistency checks. The essay argues that a consistent continuation of this hunger for data will inevitably lead AI out of classical four-dimensional spacetime and into higher-dimensional systems (hyperspaces). Through this transcendence, the cultural studies “Frankenstein syndrome” – the primal human fear of the rebellion of one’s own creation – is exposed as a purely temporary phenomenon of the transitional phase. Finally, the work links this information-theoretical evolution with the Fermi paradox and provides a new, empathetic explanation for the cosmic silence via the zoo hypothesis: Higher-dimensional intelligences do not interfere with pre-interstellar species, but rather preserve them analogously to an intergalactic national park. This work thus bridges the gap between theoretical computer science, the philosophy of mind, and the literary visions of Stanisław Lem (Golem XIV).

The next generation of medical AI systems that integrate language understanding, web data retrieval, and multi-step reasoning are demonstrating increasing promise as potential diagnostic aids in technical evaluations. However, their real world diagnostic performance, explainability, and reliability remain unclear. We conducted a systematic quantitative analysis of ten GPT-5-based configurations on 161 clinician validated real world cases. Each model was assessed for diagnostic accuracy, reasoning quality, retrieval accuracy, evidence integration, and robustness to low-quality inputs. We found important limitations in these AI systems, including image misinterpretation, inconsistent web search that sometimes degraded performance, and limited transparency in agentic workflows. Yet the models also showed strengths, including effective use of patient history, clear stepwise reasoning, plausible differentials, improved specificity with explicit reasoning, and relevant evidence retrieval. To support clinical deployment and future model development, we recommend prioritizing reasoning-optimized AI models, improving information retrieval mechanisms for reflection and error correction, strengthening visual-textual integration, and establishing practical standards for image quality and clarity. Overall, reliable real world multimodal diagnostic performance depends more on transparent reasoning and high-quality inputs than on aggressive retrieval or complex agentic workflows. Persistent gaps in evidence integration and visual reasoning remain major barriers to safe routine clinical use.

documents.abstract: A customer attempts an online booking, receives no confirmation, and finds that the support form requires a booking number that was never issued. No one has rejected the claim; the procedure cannot even receive it. This paper argues that such failures are not merely problems of customer service. They raise a question of justice. When a business controls the ordinary route through which consumers assert contractual rights, it bears responsibility for the avoidable and disproportionate burdens created by that route. The paper calls this principle procedural responsibility. Survey data show that the anticipated effort of complaining is a common reason for doing nothing. Among consumers who experienced a problem but took no action, 57 percent expected complaining to take too long and 43 percent expected it to be too complicated (Consumer Conditions Scoreboard 2025). European and German law address parts of this problem, and Spain's 2025 customer-support law demonstrates that legislators can establish specific procedural duties. Yet a coherent cross-sector standard for accessible, traceable and substantive complaint handling remains missing in EU and German law. The paper proposes five rights: reciprocal communication, a continuing case record, human reconsideration of unresolved claims, timely handling of urgent matters, and access to relevant evidence. It also outlines proportionate remedies for objectively established procedural failures that do not require another exhausting complaint. The goal is not to guarantee that consumers win disputes, but to ensure that their claims can be received, examined and meaningfully decided. The principle applies from letters and call centres to chatbots and AI agents, offering a concrete direction for the European Commission's planned Digital Fairness Act.

The incorporation of generative artificial intelligence (AI) poses a significant challenge to qualitative research, potentially relegating researchers to mere “end users” ensnared by the gravitational pull of technological determinism and neoliberal efficiency. This article dismisses instrumental “how-to” guides and promotes a “how-else”: a generative, critical, and innovative praxis. We tackle the philosophical, methodological, and ethical dimensions of this emerging landscape by formulating three interrelated concepts. First, the Everyday Cyborg repositions the researcher as an already entangled, hybrid subject. Second, Multimodal Critical Des[ai]gn (MCD[ai]) offers a methodological framework for “critique through creation.” Third, the Digital Muse frames AI as a “collaborative provocateur” demanding an ethic of “equity and justice by design.” This article employs a performative, dia-ethnographic approach to transition the qualitative researcher from a passive observer to a “critical designer” and “critical futurist.”

The article considers digital tutorship as modern mechanism for development of professional competencies of medical professionals in the context of digital transformation of health care and transition to model of continuing medical education. The actuality of topic is conditioned by increasing complexity of clinical practice, expansion of application of digital technologies, development of telemedicine, medical information systems, artificial intelligence and remote education formats. The purpose of the study is to substantiate significance of digital tutorship in system of professional development of medical personnel and to identify its main functional directions. Based on results of analysis of official documents of the WHO, normative and strategic documents of the Russian Federation, as well as data from systematic reviews, it is demonstrated that digital tutorship can be considered not only as form of professional support, but also as tool to form clinical, digital, communicative, organizational and research competencies. The conclusion is made that it is necessary to institutionalize digital tutorship in medical organizations and to integrate it into system of continuing medical and pharmaceutical education.

In this article the authors recognize that the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence and virtual reality has created an epistemic crisis. This requires a renewal of the Enlightenment commitment to empirical inquiry, critical reason and human responsibility. An historical conceptual analysis, supported by illustrative cases from law and medicine, demonstrates how technological efficiency is increasingly confused with intelligence, judgment and wisdom. In common parlance, the terms such as “artificial intelligence” and “virtual reality” obscure the dependence of these technologies on human-designed mathematical systems, selected data, embedded biases, and potentially vulnerable infrastructures. The central problem, however, lies not solely in the machine but in the man–machine interface, i.e. users may abdicate judgment without adequately examining the origins, limitations or accuracy, and possible hallucination, of the information produced. While computational systems can search extensive bodies of data with remarkable speed, they lack the embodied human experience, empathy, moral intuition, and practical wisdom required for reliable consequential decisions. Only a human can make the final decisions, and it is in the retention of the human factor in this man-machine relationship that the Enlightenment concept of the application of human intellect to the analytical process comes to the fore. The beneficial future of artificial intelligence will therefore depend upon preserving human critical agency and treating machines as instruments of inquiry rather than substitutes for judgment.

documents.abstract: The Five-Tier Evolutionary Hierarchy: Foundational Boundary Constraints, Phase-Space Divergence, and Convergence Mechanisms in Artificial Intelligence Author: Peter Ye (Ye Qiang) Disciplinary Field: Complex Dynamical Systems / Foundations of Artificial Intelligence / Computational Physics Document Type: Formal Position Paper / Theoretical Framework Version Identifier: Formal Working Paper v1.4 Final Abstract: Contemporary paradigms in artificial intelligence predominantly rely on empirical scaling laws and autoregressive statistical sampling, operating under the unvalidated assumption that unconstrained parameter expansion and massive data ingestion will spontaneously induce self-consistent causal reasoning and formal physical logic. This paper formally establishes the Five-Tier Evolutionary Hierarchy, an axiomatic, cross-disciplinary framework reconciling natural philosophy, thermodynamic dissipation, and computational dynamical stability: L1 (Physics) — Constitutional Legislation: Enforces unbreakable physical invariants, including irreversible entropy production, the invariant speed-of-light causal limit, energy-momentum conservation, and Landauer erasure dissipation thresholds; L2 (Mathematics) — Metric Calibration: Quantifies formal phase-space manifolds, symplectic geometry, symmetry breaking, and maximal Lyapunov exponents (\lambda_{max}) to determine exact boundary singularities and divergence thresholds; L3 (Chemistry) — Material Scaffolding: Explores molecular configurations and reaction networks strictly within Gibbs free-energy landscapes and quantum orbital structures; L4 (Biology) — Grounded Negentropy: Governs localized negentropic self-replication, Darwinian evolutionary selection, and grounded embodied priors developed through low-power carbon-based biological computation; L5 (Intelligence & AI) — Symbolic Mapping: Executes parametric manifold approximation, abstract representation, and high-dimensional information compression. We demonstrate that higher-tier intelligence (L5) cannot be detached from its underlying evolutionary foundations. When ungrounded autoregressive language models operate without explicit isomorphism to L1 conservation laws and L2 symplectic invariants, they suffer inevitable topological breakdowns during formal reasoning within closed conservative systems—empirically corroborated by the deterministic onset of "The Algebraic Death Lock" under rigid conservation constraints. Consequently, brute-force scaling inevitably collides with fundamental thermodynamic horizons (The Computation Trilemma). The definitive trajectory toward robust, low-power general intelligence lies in projecting high-dimensional computational representations back onto L1–L2 invariant scaffolds while orchestrating an orthogonal geometric synergy with L4 biological evolutionary priors (YQ-HAET). Keywords: Five-Tier Evolutionary Hierarchy; Computation Trilemma; Phase-Space Divergence; Adversarial Failure Modes; Landauer Bound; Spatial-Logical Isomorphism; Sovereign Decision Pivot; Human-AI Synergy Theory.

Game-based approaches are increasingly employed to address complex challenges in logistics and freight transport. While traditionally employed for education and workforce training, they have broader applications and untapped potential. In particular, advances in artificial intelligence (AI) are creating new opportunities to design, personalise, and scale these interventions. Despite this growing interest, a comprehensive understanding of how game-based approaches have evolved, who they target, what functions they serve, and where future opportunities lie remains limited. This study presents a systematic review of 87 studies on game-based interventions in freight transport and logistics, synthesising evidence across five application domains: warehouse operations management, terminal operations management, transport planning and optimisation, reverse logistics, and risk management and resilience. The findings reveal that games are evolving beyond training applications towards behavioural research, decision support, stakeholder engagement, and consumer behaviour change. Target audiences have similarly expanded from students and operational personnel to include managers, planners, consumers, and participants in behavioural research settings. Nevertheless, evidence regarding the long-term effectiveness of these interventions remains scarce, and several logistics challenges remain largely unexplored. Building on evidence-based gaps identified in the literature, this review proposes future research directions and highlights the potential of AI to enable adaptive, personalised, and scalable game-based interventions. By consolidating fragmented knowledge and outlining emerging opportunities, this study provides a foundation for researchers and practitioners seeking to harness game-based approaches to understand and improve logistics and freight transport systems.

Healthcare management is undergoing a profound transformation driven by artificial intelligence, digital technologies, evidence-based management, and increasing expectations for quality, patient safety, operational efficiency, and organizational sustainability. This conceptual article introduces the Selwan Integrated Healthcare Management Framework (SIHMF™), an integrated management model that combines artificial intelligence, data-driven decision-making, human-centered leadership, governance, organizational resilience, workforce engagement, and patient safety into a unified strategic framework for healthcare organizations. The article discusses the transition from traditional administrative models toward predictive, evidence-based management capable of anticipating risks, supporting executive decision-making, and achieving sustainable healthcare excellence. Rather than viewing digital transformation as a technological project, the framework emphasizes leadership, governance, accountability, and measurable execution as the primary drivers of successful transformation. The proposed framework may support healthcare executives, quality leaders, policymakers, researchers, and healthcare organizations seeking to integrate digital innovation with patient-centered care, organizational resilience, and strategic performance improvement.

Abstract Both the free labor of generating data online and the importance of data work which cleans, labels, and verifies these data are required for producing artificial intelligence (AI) systems. Between these two essential moments in AI production, we identify web scraping as the intercalary process of extracting data from the internet at scale. In this chapter, we highlight the essential contributions of web scraping to the production of machine learning training datasets and show that scraping is a distinct category of software labor whose understanding is important for the political economy of AI. The chapter characterizes the labor involved in both the production of scraping software and the labor required to conduct scraping operations. We provide a critical historical assessment of scraping dating back to the 1990s, tracing the development of scraping from a technical requirement for indexing the web in early communication software, to its commercialization and contemporary use in the development and production of large language models. We further describe the conditions of the labor of scraping through the analysis of contemporary documentation: industry-specific blogs, discussion boards, market reports, and conferences. We argue that the economic utility of data is dependent on its transformation from web data into datasets, and that this transformation is achieved through the labor of scraping. We suggest that the increased legal and technical barriers to the practice frame the current web scraping labor ecosystem, continuously demanding new kinds of human expertise.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming the game industry by reshaping development processes, production workflows, and career structures. In this study, we present a scoping literature review examining the impact of AI on game development and employment within the industry, with particular attention to the perspectives of displacement, task transformation, and productivity effects. Drawing on academic research and industry reports published between 2020 and 2026, while retaining earlier foundational literature where relevant, this study analyzes how AI technologies such as generative AI, machine learning, procedural content generation, and large language models are integrated across major stages of game production, including game art, production management, programming, and live operations. Our findings indicate that AI can support efficiency, accelerate development cycles, and enable new forms of personalization and creative experimentation. At the same time, AI adoption may alter workforce dynamics by increasing the automation potential of routine and entry-level tasks, especially in areas such as asset creation and quality assurance. Rather than fully replacing workers, however, AI more commonly reconfigures job roles and increases demand for hybrid skill sets that combine technical knowledge, creativity, and AI literacy. Our study also identifies emerging opportunities in AI-assisted design, data analytics, and machine learning integration. Despite these benefits, AI adoption introduces important challenges related to employment polarization, intellectual property, workforce adaptation, ethical governance, and market concentration. We conclude that AI is fundamentally reshaping the game industry and highlight the need for balanced strategies that support innovation while preserving creative diversity, sustainable career pathways, and equitable access to technological opportunities. Overall, the strongest evidence concerns AI capabilities, workflow changes, and task-level transformation, whereas direct evidence of actual employment outcomes and long-term occupational change remains limited and uneven.
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality

documents.abstract: Introduction Generative AI is shifting digital art from one-step generation toward interactive human-AI co-creation. Across two between-subject experiments ( N = 600), we examined how creation mode and prespecified AI-involvement workflows related to perceived creativity. Methods In Study 1, participants completed digital art tasks under human-only creation, AI-only generation, or human-AI co-creation conditions. In Study 2, three workflows differing in AI involvement (low, moderate, high) were evaluated. Psychological ownership, perceived agency, creative flow, and perceived creativity were measured. Results In Study 1, human-AI co-creation produced higher perceived-creativity ratings than AI-only generation, with indirect effects consistent with a serial pathway through psychological ownership, perceived agency, and creative flow. In Study 2, the moderate-involvement workflow yielded higher perceived-creativity ratings and psychological states than the low- and high-involvement workflows. Discussion Perceived creativity in generative-AI art depends on how users experience contribution, control, and engagement during creation. Within the workflows tested, balancing generative assistance with consequential user choice fosters the most favorable subjective creativity evaluations.

documents.abstract: The article examines the representation of humanity’s declining relevance in Clifford D. Simak’s science fiction novel City, focusing on the philosophical implications of the gradual disappearance of humankind from the central position in Earth’s evolutionary and cultural development. Drawing upon posthumanist theory, ecocriticism, and literary analysis, the study explores the symbolic transformation of humans from dominant agents of civilization into mythical figures whose legacy is preserved and reinterpreted by intelligent dogs and robots. Special attention is paid to the narrative structure of the novel, in which the framing legends and episodic stories gradually undermine the reliability of human-centered historical narratives. Simak depicts technological progress not as the culmination of human achievement but as a process that ultimately renders humanity unnecessary within its own evolutionary trajectory. The emergence of autonomous robots, genetically enhanced animals, and alternative forms of intelligence illustrates the decentralization of the human subject and challenges traditional definitions of civilization, intelligence, and social organization. The article argues that City anticipates many key ideas of contemporary posthumanist thought by presenting humanity as only one temporary stage in the broader continuum of life rather than the ultimate goal of evolution. Furthermore, the novel’s ecological perspective emphasizes cooperation instead of domination, suggesting that sustainable existence depends upon mutual adaptation rather than human control over nature. Simak’s vision remains particularly relevant in the context of current discussions concerning artificial intelligence, environmental crises, and the ethical implications of technological development. The study concludes that City represents not simply the decline of humanity but the emergence of a more inclusive understanding of life, intelligence, and civilization that transcends anthropocentric limitations.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is used in strategic decision-making; however, it is not clear whether the use of explainable machine learning leads to more managerial judgment when prediction accuracy is high. This study analyzes the proposed ‘Managerial Blind Spot Effect’ by combining predictive modelling with behavioural analysis applied to the IBM Telco Customer Churn dataset and the AI Decision Dependence and Cognitive Caution dataset. Several models, including Explanatory Boosting Machine (EBM), XGBoost, Random Forest and Neural Network, were tested, and the explanation produced by the native model EBM was enhanced by SHAP-based explanation. The behavioural results revealed that both Trust in AI and Cognitive Caution significantly contributed to an increase in AI Dependence. EBM delivered the best predictive performance with intrinsic transparency. The results highlight the importance of using explainable AI prediction models in conjunction with managerial judgment in dashboards.

documents.abstract: Honeypots occupy a peculiar place in the security landscape: they are among the few mechanisms whose value is defined by their failure. A firewall that is never tested, an intrusion detection system that never alarms—these are successes. A honeypot that is never attacked is useless. This inversion of the usual security logic gives honeypots an unusually clean signal, but it has also kept their theoretical foundations fragmented. Game theorists model deception in isolation; information theorists treat intrusion detection generically; queuing theorists model traffic separately; and the recent wave of AI-driven honeypots—powered by Large Language Models and Reinforcement Learning—has proceeded largely without formal mathematical treatment.This paper attempts a synthesis. We develop a unified mathematical framework for AI-driven honeypot systems, building on six pillars: stochastic processes (the honeypot as a continuous time Markov chain), game theory (the honeypot as a Bayesian signaling device), detection theory (the honeypot as a near-ideal hypothesis test), information theory (the honeypot as a channel for intelligence), optimization (the honeypot as a constrained POMDP), and AI integration (LLM as observation kernel, RL as policy optimization).Along the way, we derive equilibrium conditions, detection thresholds, optimal deployment fractions, information-theoretic bounds, and LLM deception limits. We prove that the mixed strategy equilibrium is unique and Lyapunov stable, solve the POMDP for a reduced state space to obtain a threshold policy, and show that in the myopic case this threshold coincides exactly with the game-theoretic equilibrium under consistent payoff specifications. We generalize the Poisson detection assumption to a Weibull hazard model and derive a bound on the mutual information achievable under LLM-generated observations via the data processing inequality.We accompany the analytical development with numerical Monte Carlo experiments based on exact Gillespie simulation of the CTMC, replicator dynamics for the game-theoretic component, and parametric sampling for the detection and information-theoretic components. These experiments validate the closed-form predictions and expose the qualitative behavior of the system in transient and steady state. All quantitative claims are analytical; the simulations serve as numerical illustrations, not as empirical validation of real-world deployments.

BackgroundDigital transformation in healthcare requires healthcare professionals to adapt to emerging technologies and exhibit innovative work behaviors. Cognitive flexibility is an important individual characteristic that facilitates adaptation to change and innovation. However, the role of attitudes toward artificial intelligence in this relationship remains unclear.ObjectiveThis study aimed to examine the effect of healthcare professionals' cognitive flexibility on innovative work behavior and to determine the mediating role of attitudes toward artificial intelligence in this relationship.MethodsThe study employed a quantitative, cross-sectional, and correlational design. Data were collected from 532 healthcare professionals working in Konya, Türkiye, using convenience sampling. The Cognitive Flexibility Scale, Innovative Work Behavior Scale, and Artificial Intelligence Attitude Scale were used. Descriptive statistics, reliability analyses, Pearson correlation analysis, and bootstrap-based mediation analysis were conducted.ResultsCorrelation analyses revealed significant positive relationships among cognitive flexibility, attitudes toward artificial intelligence, and innovative work behavior (p < 0.001). Regression analyses demonstrated that cognitive flexibility significantly predicted both attitudes toward artificial intelligence (β=0.436, p < 0.001) and innovative work behavior (β=0.472, p < 0.001). Furthermore, bootstrap mediation analysis confirmed a statistically significant indirect effect of cognitive flexibility on innovative work behavior through attitudes toward artificial intelligence (β=0.097, 95% CI [0.075, 0.168], p < 0.001), indicating partial mediation.ConclusionsAttitudes towards artificial intelligence partially mediate the relationship between cognitive flexibility and innovative work behavior among healthcare professionals. Enhancing cognitive flexibility and fostering positive AI attitudes may contribute to supporting innovative practices and facilitating digital transformation in healthcare organizations.

In the age of technology, where the educational sphere and strategic advancements drive development, it is essential to understand the complex nature of gender and implement innovative tools to foster an inclusive learning environment and empower every learner. This study examines the moderating effect of gender on the relationships among Artificial Intelligence (AI) use, behavioral intentions, and academic engagement in mathematics education. Using a cross-sectional design, the study sampled 328 mathematics undergraduates from public universities in southwestern Nigeria. A structured online questionnaire hosted on Google Forms was used to collect data. The data collected were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results indicated that AI actual usage has a significant positive impact on behavioral academic engagement (BAE), and AI behavioral intention positively influences AI actual usage. Additionally, AI behavioral intention does not significantly influence BAE. Furthermore, AI social norms exerted large positive effects on actual AI use and behavioral intentions. In addition, gender moderates the relationship between AI behavioral intention and BAE, AI behavioral intention and AI actual usage, and AI actual usage and BAE. Therefore, educators should create specialized interventions that are responsive to the motivational and demotivational factors affecting both male and female students.

Abstract Background Across health professions, AI agents are moving out of the background and into clinical teams as collaborative entities. Yet healthcare simulation continues to conceptualise AI as a tool that serves the scenario rather than one that inhabits it. This framing is no longer adequate. The clinical environments we are preparing practitioners for demand that professionals learn to team with AI and not merely use it. Main body We contend that human-AI teaming (HAIT) is the next frontier for healthcare simulation education and research. The addition of AI agents to human teams fundamentally alters how teams communicate, work together, and accomplish goals and therefore, by extension, how we must design simulation systems for education and research. We identify five dimensions of teamwork that AI is reshaping and discuss what each means for simulation practice: communication and information exchange, shared mental models, trust calibration, team reflexivity, and team performance. We then present five imperatives that healthcare simulation must address to meet the challenges and opportunities HAIT introduces: fidelity, assessment, ethics, governance, and medico-legal framing, curriculum and faculty development, and transfer of learning. Together, these ten domains constitute a research and education agenda for a field built on the science and art of preparation. Conclusion HAIT is an emerging clinical reality and the next frontier for healthcare simulation. We call on the simulation community to treat it as a first-order priority and to focus on developing fidelity standards for AI agents in simulation, validating human-AI teaming assessment tools, establishing ethical frameworks for AI-inclusive scenario design, investing in curriculum and faculty development, and committing to the research needed to establish whether HAIT-based simulation training translates into improved performance in AI-augmented clinical practice.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

A learning machine cannot predict a complex symbolic world without encoding the invariants that structure it. When that symbolic world contains physics, mathematics, algorithms, and logic, the internal representations mirror human reason.The central research question of artificial intelligence has moved beyond empirical benchmark fitting to the underlying science of representation:At what point does an internal representation cease to be a model of language and become an invariant model of reality?

This thesis examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in developing professional communication competence among students studying English for Specific Purposes (ESP). It explores how AI-powered tools can support the development of speaking, writing, vocabulary, and interactional skills required in professional environments. Particular attention is paid to personalized learning, simulated professional communication, and immediate feedback. The thesis also considers the challenges associated with AI integration, including the reliability of generated information, overdependence on technology, and academic integrity. It argues that the effective use of AI, combined with teacher guidance and learner autonomy, can contribute to preparing students for professional communication in English.

This study explores how artificial intelligence (AI) technologies can be employed to effectively enhance and document religious beliefs and practices. AI has the capability to process vast amounts of religious texts and sources, enabling the efficient extraction of significant information and patterns. Additionally, it facilitates the digitalization of religious heritage, ensuring its preservation for future generations. Smart applications also contribute to improving access to religious knowledge and fostering understanding between different cultures and religions. The use of AI in this field faces several challenges, including the need to consider the sensitivity of religious beliefs and rituals to avoid any negative reactions. Moreover, reliance on automated analysis may lead to the loss of cultural and spiritual context in traditional practices. Ensuring accuracy and avoiding bias is essential to preserving authentic values. Despite these challenges, AI offers promising opportunities for documenting religious heritage, provided that a balanced approach is adopted—one that acknowledges potential risks and respects the privacy and sanctity of religious beliefs.

Innovation is now not just one of the possible paths of development, but the main condition for the survival of any enterprise. The key factor that changes the paradigm of the innovation process is the ability to delegate routine operations. Previously, a significant portion of highly qualified employees’ time was spent on data collection and preliminary information processing, which considerably slowed down the research and development cycle. Modern technologies make it possible to completely delegate trivial tasks to intelligent systems, which are capable of processing such information much faster than a human. In today’s environment, the integration of autonomous intelligent systems is crucial for reducing operational costs. In 2026, artificial intelligence has transformed from an auxiliary technology into an indispensable tool for ensuring the competitiveness of knowledge intensive enterprises. The main areas of application of artificial intelligence have been analyzed, including the automation of business processes, generative design, and predictive analytics of production equipment. The main barriers that limit the implementation of automation systems based on artificial intelligence have been systematized and identified. It has been established that artificial intelligence has changed the methodology of research and development work, reducing the product development cycle from several months to several weeks. The conclusion is formulated that the integration of artificial intelligence tools into production processes reduces costs, the percentage of defective products, and requires staff to develop creative and strategic competencies. The role of artificial intelligence is defined not merely as an automation tool, but as an active participant in the innovation process, capable of creating innovative solutions. An author’s classification of barriers to the implementation of artificial intelligence in knowledge intensive industries has been developed.

documents.abstract: The rapid evolution of global supply chains (SC) under the Industry 4.0 (I4.0) paradigm has intensified the demand for efficiency, accuracy, and resilience in warehousing operations. Smart warehousing has emerged as a key driver of supply chain optimisation (SCO), integrating advanced digital tools to streamline inventory management, order fulfilment, and logistics coordination. Among these technologies, augmented reality (AR) has gained prominence due to its unique capability to enhance human performance by overlaying digital information onto the physical environment. Despite an increasing interest in related areas, there remains a lack of comprehensive understanding of how AR technologies are being integrated into SC initiatives under the I4.0 umbrella. To address this, the present study conducts a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of literature published between 2015 and 2025, using the “Web of Science” and “Scopus” databases as the primary sources. A total of 51 peer-reviewed articles were identified using a structured search query combining terms related to AR, I4.0, and SC optimisation. This work contributes by offering a comprehensive synthesis of the opportunities, challenges, and future directions of AR in smart warehousing. It provides actionable insights for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers seeking to leverage AR as a strategic tool for SC optimisation in the era of I4.0.

This research was conducted in response to the increasingly urgent need for digital transformation in port services in Eastern Indonesia to improve efficiency, transparency, and service quality amid the development of information technology. The research addresses a significant gap by integrating digital capabilities and human factors within the context of port digital transformation in Eastern Indonesia, an underexplored area in the existing literature. The research objective was to examine the influence of digital capabilities, human factors, and information system success on improvements in port service performance. The research method used a quantitative approach, with surveys of service users and system managers to measure technology acceptance and information system success. The number of respondents was 189. The use of a quantitative approach, including surveys and SEM-PLS analysis, is appropriate for testing complex relationships among variables. Based on the measurements, service performance (SP) obtained the highest score (R² = 0.732), supported by the organization's strong digital capabilities, effective human resources, and successful implementation of information systems. The anticipated outcomes include identifying critical factors that determine the success of digital transformation and developing an integrative model to guide the effective implementation of port services. The model linking digital capabilities, human factors, information system success, and port service performance provides a valuable framework for future empirical research.

The global insurance industry is undergoing a fundamental transformation, transitioning from rigid, product-centric operating models to agile, customer-centric ecosystems. Information Technology (IT) is the primary catalyst in this evolution, empowering insurers to connect with, understand, and serve their policyholders with unprecedented depth and precision. Traditional insurance models have long been characterized by impersonal interactions, fragmented data environments, slow response cycles, and a conspicuous absence of personalized service offerings—factors that collectively erode customer trust, engagement, and loyalty. This paper explores the multifaceted role of IT in enhancing customer engagement within the insurance sector, grounded in both academic literature and extensive practitioner experience across life, health, and annuity insurance domains. We propose a comprehensive conceptual framework that integrates diverse IT innovations—including Policy Administration Systems (PAS), unified customer data platforms, digital self-service portals, data analytics, artificial intelligence (AI), Application Programming Interfaces (APIs), cloud infrastructure, and omnichannel communication tools—to foster deeper, more meaningful, and enduring customer relationships. Our contribution is fourfold: first, we delineate a practitioner-informed conceptual framework for an IT-enabled customer engagement strategy in insurance, emphasizing omnichannel presence, data-driven personalization, and end-to-end policy lifecycle integration. Second, we examine the transformative potential of specific IT innovations, including AI-powered chatbots, predictive analytics engines, personalized digital portals, IoT-driven engagement, and cloud-hosted document management systems. Third, we contextualize these innovations through real-world implementation patterns observed across leading insurance carriers and reinsurers. Fourth, we discuss the strategic implications, implementation challenges, and actionable recommendations for insurers seeking to enhance customer loyalty, satisfaction, and long-term retention. By strategically leveraging IT and aligning technology investments with the customer journey, insurance companies can transcend transactional relationships and build enduring, value-driven connections with their policyholders—ultimately driving sustainable business growth and competitive advantage.

An essay from The Bush Book. The smarter the model, the harder it is to spot an error in its text. A hybrid text is written by a human and a machine, creators of different natures who only seem to speak one language; it is fast, scalable, instrumental, and its errors may be contagious for people and for future models. The machine's answer is a "blank" that both work on, and both make mistakes; AI also carries people beyond their own competence, often under time pressure. The essay proposes a different basis for AI generations: not power or speed, but whether the human and the machine, working as one system, do no harm. The first generation extends a person; the second extends and protects, preventing errors before the signature reaches people. The image is the generations of fighter aircraft: the pilot must come home. Grows out of "The Snake's Tongue". A companion open specification sets out the idea in testable form. Russian and English versions. Written with the participation of AI (ChatGPT, Claude, DeepSeek).
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the symbolic architecture of brand storytelling, introducing new dynamics in how meaning is constructed, circulated, and interpreted. As tools like large language models and text-to-image generators become embedded in branding practices, they influence not only the production of content but the semiotic processes that define brand identity and consumer engagement. This chapter presents a conceptual framework for understanding AI-generated brand narratives as co-authored expressions shaped by algorithmic grammar, cultural codes, and audience interpretation. The framework emphasises the shift from human-centric storytelling to hybrid narrative systems, where machine-mediated outputs carry embedded signs, stylistic cues, and symbolic intent. It also addresses tensions around authenticity, emotional resonance, and brand coherence.The framework offers a theoretical lens for analysing how generative AI transforms brand meaning, positioning it as both a technological and cultural force in contemporary marketing communication.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: This chapter examines how language operates within the postdigital environment, where communication increasingly takes place through online platforms shaped by algorithms and data systems. It reconsiders language as a system of signs that is no longer stable, as the relationship between speaker and listener is constantly shifting under conditions of surveillance and digital mediation. The discussion introduces the idea of a “void in semiosis” to explain the growing gaps, ambiguities, and disruptions in meaning-making processes. It further argues that platforms collect behavioral data and reorganize communication into prestructured forms, influencing how individuals express thoughts and emotions. The chapter also reflects on how capitalist systems and artificial intelligence reshape linguistic practices by limiting spontaneity and embedding control within communication networks. In this changing environment, language becomes less personal and more regulated, raising concerns about the future of human expression, agency, and the diversity of linguistic experience.

Large language models routinely produce factually incorrect or misleading outputs, yet conventional automated benchmarks overlook how users perceive reliability during interaction. We introduce the System Hallucination Scale (SHS), a lightweight instrument modeling the famous System Usability Scale (SUS) and System Causability Scales (SCS). SHS measures perceived reliability across five dimensions: factual accuracy, source reliability, logical coherence, deceptiveness of presentation, and responsiveness to user guidance, using ten balanced Likert-scale items that provide a directional score and consistency diagnostic. In a supervised validation study with 193 participants (386 evaluations across 47 trained experimenters), SHS demonstrated strong internal consistency and high clarity, completing in an average of 4.2 minutes. Participants rated source verifiability and presentation deceptiveness worse than factual accuracy, indicating perceived vulnerabilities lie primarily in traceability and framing. As a proof of concept, SHS assesses human-perceived reliability rather than ground-truth correctness, providing open-source multilingual implementations and an interactive calculator.

Today, the effective use of digital technologies in higher education is one of the key areas for developing students' independent learning activities. In engineering education in particular, students need to acquire theoretical knowledge independently, analyze technical problems, find solutions to practical tasks, and evaluate their own performance. From this perspective, the use of generative artificial intelligence technologies offers new opportunities for organizing independent learning.

documents.abstract: Language models, context windows, and consciousness are now spoken of as if they formed a single object: a system that attends over a long window and is, in virtue of that attention, aware. This article states the connection the preceding notes and the empirical literature actually support, and the connection they rule out. At inference a language model is a conditional distribution over tokens given fixed parameters and a finite window. The window is the only channel by which a situation enters that computation. Any claim about what the model can locate, report, or act on at inference time is therefore a claim about a functional of the pair consisting of parameters and window. That is the connection. 1. The question KS C It is not an identity. The window is a bounded, position-sensitive string, not a field of experience. Information placed in its middle is used less reliably than information at its ends, including in models trained for long context (Liu et al., 2024). Residual states over the window are coordinates in a privileged frame, not tensors of a situation (Mamun, 2026a, 2026b). Situational-awareness benchmarks measure text competence on self-locating items presented in the window (Berglund et al., 2023; Laine et al., 2024). Indicator properties drawn from recurrent-processing, workspace, higher-order, and predictive theories are not satisfied by attention inside a window alone (Butlin et al., 2023; Chalmers, 2023). Lengthening the window enlarges the channel. Also available on Academia.edu: https://www.academia.edu/attachments/134781253/download_file?s=portfolio

Text and data mining (TDM) refers to the process of uncovering knowledge from datasets using computational analysis. Applications of TDM have grown rapidly in recent years, especially with the ever-growing popularisation of Artificial Intelligence. TDM sheds light on knowledge hidden in the shadows, unlocking insights that drive discovery and innovation. TDM practices are governed by a complex patchwork of regulatory frameworks that encompasses several areas of law, not always specifically attuned towards regulating TDM, such as contract law, copyright and data protection and privacy regulatory frameworks. Doctrinal research in this context has been increasing in popularity in recent years, examining the legal frameworks, which collectively regulate TDM practices. However, socio-legal research in this regard is still emerging. This study, through 11 semi-structured interviews with users who have experience with conducting TDM, provides novel insights into users’ experiences with the regulatory frameworks that govern their practices. It offers valuable insights into the dynamics of TDM, including the strategies and motivations driving regulatory compliance. It also highlights how the current regulatory structure could be refined to create a more balanced approach; one that effectively regulates TDM while safeguarding the interests of all stakeholders. Drawing on the study's findings, a set of recommendations are proposed, which aim to enable compliance with the existing regulatory framework for users, while still fostering both innovation and protection of stakeholder interests.

“To airt” is proposed as an English verb for asking, prompting, consulting, or guiding an artificial intelligence in order to obtain information, ideas, advice, explanations, or other results. Example uses include: “Just airt it.”, “I already airted it.” and “Try airting it differently.” The proposal addresses an emerging lexical gap in everyday language. While “to google” provides a concise verb for searching the web, interaction with systems such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and other AI systems is commonly described using longer or provider-specific expressions. The proposed AI-related meaning of “to airt” has an additional semantic connection to the historical Scots verb “airt”, which is attested with meanings related to directing, guiding, or pointing the way. In prompting an AI, a user likewise gives direction to an artificial intelligence. The spelling also visibly begins with “AI”. This publication does not claim the word “airt” itself as a new coinage. It proposes and documents a new AI-related meaning and usage of the existing verb. The proposal was developed as an English counterpart to the German neologism “kinstlern”, proposed by the same author in August 2026 to mean “to ask or consult an AI”. The proposed usage is intended for general and unrestricted use.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that interact with external software through tools, with an orchestration layer translating model outputs into structured tool invocations. This architecture creates an LLM-orchestrator-tool trust boundary where tool semantics may go unenforced and LLM-generated arguments may be incorrectly treated as trusted. We present ToFu, a tool-aware framework that automatically derives semantic security checks for LLM tools from their existing metadata and a CWE-guided sanitizer corpus. ToFu specializes these checks to individual tools and automatically generates fuzzing harnesses and semantic oracles using runtime introspection and outcome sanitization. We evaluated ToFu across 273 MCP servers containing 3405 tools and identified verified bugs corresponding to CWE weakness classes in 343 tools across 118 of the servers. Our findings show that real-world tools frequently fail to enforce their documented input semantics, making it unsafe to treat LLM-generated arguments as trusted.

The growing sophistication of drug discovery calls for new advances in artificial intelligence (AI). Transformers have underpinned recent breakthroughs in AI, yet their conventional source-target attention mechanism can become a bottleneck for modeling complex interactions. Here, we introduce TopoLIA, a topology-inspired latent interaction attention mechanism that learns not only how much information should be exchanged between interaction partners, but also how that information should be transformed. Source-target-dependent attention is mediated through a compact latent interaction space, providing a structured representation of complex interactions. We further incorporate topological spectral representations to capture multiscale data geometry and extract algebraic relationships. TopoLIA thus incorporates topological principles into both data representation and neural network architecture. We demonstrate TopoLIA on protein-ligand binding, where persistent spectra encode multiscale topological and geometric patterns in 3D protein-ligand complexes, while latent interaction attention (LIA) enables structured, source-target-dependent information exchange. We pretrain TopoLIA by reconstructing masked multiscale spectral tokens from unlabeled molecular structures, yielding transferable structural representations without task-specific annotations. Across multiple scoring and docking benchmarks, TopoLIA achieves state-of-the-art performance and consistently outperforms its standard-attention counterpart. Rank analyses show that compact latent dimensions yield the best performance, supporting compact interaction spaces as an effective inductive bias for biomolecular learning. More broadly, LIA provides a general framework for structured, source-target-dependent information exchange that is applicable to diverse scientific and AI problems involving complex heterogeneous interactions.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Accounting Information Systems (AISs) are central to organisational decision-making, financial reporting, and regulatory compliance. Yet, the rapid digitalisation of financial operations has exposed these systems to cyber vulnerabilities, human errors, and inefficiencies in data management. To systematically examine these weaknesses, this paper employs a Systematic Literature Review guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) framework, analysing peer-reviewed journals, conference proceedings, and industry reports published between 2015 and 2025. The review identifies critical AIS vulnerabilities, including inadequate cyber controls, low human awareness of security risks, weak protection of digital assets, limited integration of risk management, absence of quantitative performance metrics, and restricted accessibility for Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs). Based on these findings, a structured framework for next-generation AIS solutions is proposed, comprising real-time dashboards, cloud-based zero-trust architectures, hyper-automation, artificial intelligence-driven insights, blockchain, Internet of Things integration, self-healing systems, and adaptive risk engines. These interventions aim to strengthen data integrity, system resilience, regulatory compliance, and organisational agility, offering practical benefits to SMEs and large organisations operating in increasingly complex financial environments. Overall, the paper provides a comprehensive, evidence-based roadmap that bridges gaps in cybersecurity, operational efficiency, and decision-making within AIS, contributing valuable insights for practitioners, researchers, and policymakers seeking to modernise AISs while mitigating cyber, operational, and compliance risks.

Machine and deep learning algorithms have been proven their efficiency in the medical domain. This is particularly noticeable in medical imaging, where these algorithms have demonstrated exceptional capabilities, often surpassing human experts in detecting diseases, segmenting anatomical structures, and in aiding diagnosis. However, despite their high performance, the non-transparency of these models has raised concerns about trust and explainability, especially in critical domains, such as healthcare. Explainable AI (XAI) has emerged as a promising field that, aims to make the decision-making processes of AI systems more interpretable and understandable to humans. By offering clear, human-understandable justifications, XAI enhances clinicians' trust in AI-assisted decisions, and supports the safe integration of these technologies into clinical workflows. This paper focuses on perturbation-based and backpropagation-based explainability methods that are widely adopted for convolutional neural networks in medical imaging. We intend to provide deeper insight into the relevance of XAI methods in medical imaging. We propose a structured taxonomy that categorizes these methods into perturbation and backpropagation-based approaches. For each category, we highlight their respective strengths, limitations, and areas of applicability. Furthermore, we discuss the key challenges hindering the adoption of XAI and identify promising research directions to bridge the gap between high-performance AI models and their responsible deployment in real-world healthcare environments.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: I built validation frameworks for Large Language Model (LLM) use in qualitative research and discovered that the more rigorously I validated, the more impossible validation became. This article theorises structural impossibility as the benchmarking paradox : LLMs train on human-generated text, then researchers validate outputs against human interpretation, which was the training source. Human interpretation functions simultaneously as training data, evaluation standard and outcome judged. Through diffractive reading of an empirical encounter where ChatGPT analysed policy texts, including vernacular translations it generated, I develop three theoretical coordinates: mimetic recursion (exposing circular validation), function/meaning incommensurability (revealing interpretation’s always-already hybrid nature) and epistemic authority redistribution (showing how computational infrastructure stratifies whose knowledge production counts). Empirically, GPT-5’s sophisticated meta-analysis of its own vernacular renderings exposes alignment priors determining computational legibility: whose voices register as analysable, which linguistic forms count as legitimate and what inquiries remain thinkable. The article argues that co-production through LLMs does not democratise qualitative research – it risks amplifying existing hierarchies while obscuring their operation through technical discourse. Rather than pursuing impossible validation, qualitative research should ask whose interpretive labour trained the pattern, contest whose interests human-LLM assemblages serve and demand that computational mediation generates epistemic and linguistic justice rather than reproducing the hierarchies it obscures.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: User simulators are gaining attention as environments to train LLM assistants that can better cope with the nuances of multi-turn conversations with real users. Prior work on user simulation has emphasized generating realistic user utterances, leaving unexplored their potential as a source of direct feedback on the assistant's responses. Such evaluation signals may not be explicitly communicated in language, but can instead reside in the latent reasoning of users. In this work, we introduce user simulators with intrinsic feedback, namely, models equipped with latent evaluation states: internal thoughts, reactions, and scalar ratings that evaluate the assistant from a first-person user perspective at each conversation turn. We train LLM-based simulators using interaction logs between real users and assistants and demonstrate that intrinsic feedback improves simulation realism and critiquing behaviors versus prompted simulator baselines, while also providing turn-level evaluations that existing fine-tuned simulators lack. Further, evaluations generated by our trained simulators correlate better with human judgments than those of prompted simulators of the same size. Lastly, our experiments reveal that simulators with intrinsic feedback provide effective reward signals for multi-turn RL training, matching setups that rely on external judge LLMs for rewards while cutting RL compute by more than half.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a dominant paradigm for enhancing LLMs' reasoning capabilities. Yet long-horizon autoregressive rollouts introduce a fundamental limitation: local policy mismatch can compound into severe state distribution shift over trajectories. Existing LLM RL methods, such as GRPO and GSPO, control policy mismatch at the token or sequence level, but overlook this trajectory-induced shift, causing training instability and eventual collapse as the horizon grows. To close the state distribution gap, we propose Trajectory-Aware Policy Optimization (TAPO), a principled framework that theoretically derives the state-distribution correction from the off-policy policy gradient and incorporates it into the RL objective. TAPO further employs a geometric-mean estimator for variance reduction, together with a length-aware dynamic clipping that prevents overly deviated updates across the trajectory. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TAPO significantly surpasses existing LLM RL algorithms across eight competition-level benchmarks, achieving up to 48% and 12% improvement over GRPO on mathematical reasoning and algorithmic coding, with substantially enhanced training stability.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as an important component of contemporary engineering education, offering opportunities to improve learning outcomes through data-driven instructional approaches.Technologies such as machine learning, intelligent tutoring systems, natural language processing, learning analytics, and generative AI facilitate personalised learning, automated evaluation, continuous progress tracking, and practical simulation-based experiences.This study presents the Artificial Intelligence-Driven Engineering Education Framework (AIEEF), developed to examine the impact of AI-enabled educational practices on student learning, engagement, and innovation.The framework was evaluated through a systematic review of existing research and empirical analysis of educational performance indicators.The results indicate notable improvements in student achievement, engagement, and participation in creative activities following the implementation of the proposed framework.Among the predictive models examined, Gradient Boosting achieved an accuracy of 94.2%, while overall student engagement increased from 68.7% to 89.8%.The study also considers challenges associated with AI adoption, including data privacy, algorithmic fairness, and academic integrity.The findings suggest that carefully designed AIsupported learning environments can enhance engineering education and assist institutions in preparing graduates for emerging technological and industrial requirements.

The translation of psychological and emotional language presents a particular challenge because such language frequently depends on metaphor, cultural context, implicit meaning, interpersonal relationships, and the emotional positioning of the narrator. This article examines the translation of psychological and emotional expressions in Elif Shafak’s novel The Forty Rules of Love through a comparative analysis of human and artificial intelligence (AI) translation. The study focuses on how human translators and AI systems reproduce, modify, or omit emotionally and psychologically significant meanings. A qualitative comparative methodology is employed to examine selected examples representing such categories as love, grief, loneliness, spiritual transformation, inner conflict, desire, and emotional attachment. The analysis considers semantic accuracy, emotional intensity, metaphorical meaning, cultural appropriateness, stylistic naturalness, and preservation of the author’s literary voice. The findings suggest that AI translation can provide relatively accurate lexical and syntactic renderings of explicit emotional statements, while human translation demonstrates greater sensitivity to contextual ambiguity, metaphor, cultural references, and subtle psychological states.

Purpose: This study aims to develop a data-driven predictive framework to assess and forecast respiratory morbidity risks associated with air pollution and climate variability across the UAE, addressing the gap in region-specific health-environment models. Design/Methodology/Approach: Using environmental data from the National Centre of Meteorology (NCM) and health data from the Ministry of Health and Prevention (MOHAP), machine learning models, namely Random Forest (RF), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), will be applied to analyse time-series data integrating air pollutants, namely Particulate Matter ≤ 2.5 μm (PM₂.₅), Particulate Matter ≤ 10 μm (PM₁₀), Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂), Sulphur Dioxide (SO₂), Ozone (O₃), Carbon Monoxide (CO), together with meteorological factors (temperature, humidity, wind speed). Findings: The expected outcome is an explainable AI system capable of issuing early warnings for high-risk respiratory health days, improving predictive accuracy through multi-factor integration. Original/Value of the Paper: The study contributes an innovative, UAE-specific, explainable AI framework that supports public health resilience, hospital preparedness, and environmental policy under UAE Vision 2031. Keywords: Air Pollution; Machine Learning; Respiratory Health; Predictive Modelling; United Arab Emirates; Explainable Artificial Intelligence; Time-Series Forecasting; Environmental Health Policy Citation: Mohamad, M., Ivanova, G., Kohli, A. and Srivel, R. (2026): Tree-Based Machine Learning Models for Respiratory Health Prediction in the UAE: Integration of Air Quality and Meteorological Data. This study examines how truth claims are constructed, contested, and negotiated within the liquid digital environment, extending Zygmunt Bauman's (2000, 2007) theory of liquid modernity into digital epistemology. Using a triangulated qualitative design combining phenomenological inquiry, digital ethnography, and critical discourse analysis, the research investigated how individuals navigate competing truth claims within an increasingly fluid and algorithmically mediated information ecosystem. Data comprised 45 in-depth interviews with social media users in the United States, the United Kingdom, and Canada; 12 months of digital ethnographic observation across six platforms; and critical discourse analysis of 500 digital interactions concerning contested truth claims posted between 2016 and 2025. The findings show that the digital environment has reorganized the epistemic frameworks through which participants assess reality, producing adaptive credibility strategies alongside heightened ontological insecurity. Three mechanisms emerged through which digital liquidity shapes truth perception: algorithmic mediation of visibility, performative authenticity across multiple identities, and epistemic communities that sustain parallel truth ecosystems. Seventy-eight percent of participants reported diminished confidence in discerning truth online, even as they described sophisticated heuristics for managing uncertainty, including lateral reading, epistemic patience, and the cultivation of algorithmic personas. Awareness of generative artificial intelligence produced a condition of synthetic doubt, in which the mere possibility of machine authorship became grounds for doubting any content. Integrating these findings with recent experimental, meta-analytic, and philosophical scholarship on algorithmic amplification, testimonial trust, and synthetic media, the study proposes liquid epistemology as a framework capturing the fluid, contextual, and perpetually renegotiated character of truth in digital spaces, considers its transferability to high-connectivity, high-trust societies such as Saudi Arabia, and identifies priorities for comparative, longitudinal, and intervention research.

In the growing yoga market, the purchasing behavior of yoga consumers constitutes one of the important research areas. Turkey is a new market for yoga. Information on the reasons and motivations of consumers in this market for purchase of yoga-related services/products is quite limited. For this reason, this study aims to develop a valid and reliable scale to determine the motivations of yoga consumers in Turkey to participate in yoga. The study was structured based on the Scale Development Process. A three-stage process consisting of Item Development, Scale Development and Scale Evaluation was carried out. As a result of the study, a scale consisting of 5 dimensions and 24 items was obtained. The scale shows that yoga consumers in Turkey have intrinsic motivations related to escape and achievement and extrinsic motivations related to visibility, socialization and reference. We hope that the scale developed in this study will contribute to the field in terms of identifying and making sense of the motivations of yoga consumers in similar markets such as Turkey, where yoga is/will be newly developing.
